extracted.intended_audience: students enrolled in the IWP seven-week online fiction workshop / international writers participating in the IWP online courses
extracted.subtask_description: A seven-week online fiction seminar linking US and international writers that combines reading, weekly creative and academic responses, one longer workshop story, peer critiques, and weekly real-time videoconference workshops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop piece — fiction (length & completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: One during the seminar, each student will compose an 8-10 page story for class critique. Each piece must be “complete” in that it must have a beginning, middle, and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pieces must be final draft quality (no grammatical errors, misspellings, and so on). Submit according to the weekly schedule (participants post by Tuesday in designated weeks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative responses (mini-essays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four times throughout the semester, you will be asked to take a little excursion and then write a 350-400 word mini-essay about that experience, employing a particular element of craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative responses should employ a specific craft element from the Writer’s Toolkit and may be fused into your workshop essay. Post to CourseKit/ICON by the stated deadline (often Monday of the week following the prompt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic responses to discussion questions
rubrics_metrics.description: For each of the books/readings the instructors will post probing discussion questions; students must write an original response of 350-400 thoughtful, well-reasoned words to one of the questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also write a brief ~100 word response to one classmate's response where required. Responses must be completed by the deadline (e.g., Monday of the week following the posting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop responses / letters of critique (timing & focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every student will respond to each workshop contribution via a letter of critique within a week of the story’s submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques should focus on elements of craft—style, character, voice, dialogue, and so on—and should provide insightful, detailed, and specific criticism on how to improve the piece. In the fiction seminar, responses to participants’ stories are generally ~350 words; in other courses a 1-page response is used. All responses should be polite, considerate, and constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and tone of peer feedback (etiquette)
rubrics_metrics.description: All responses should be polite, considerate, and constructive. Any student who routinely violates this policy may face a grade reduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feedback must be detailed and specific (not merely 'I liked it'); explain how to improve craft elements. Maintain professional workshop etiquette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation (presence & contribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are expected to maintain an active presence on the discussion boards and in videoconference sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For undergraduates, the final letter grade will be largely determined by how extensively you participate in discussions (forums and video chat) and the quality of your feedback. Auditors/non-credit students: essays will only be workshopped if you generously participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadlines and lateness policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Lateness of an assignment will adversely impact your final grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments have specified due dates (e.g., creative and academic responses due by Monday of the week following the posting; workshop pieces posted by Tuesday in assigned weeks; critiques within one week). Instructors reserve the right to request documentation for missed work due to illness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical & platform requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: As this is a web-based class, students will need a high-speed internet connection, access to a webcam and microphone, and CourseKit/ICON and Elluminate for video chat sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text materials are sourced from online journals (no purchase necessary). Make sure you can reliably connect to live sessions and post to the course platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final draft quality standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshop submissions must be 'final draft quality,' meaning no grammatical errors, misspellings, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors expect pieces to be polished before submission; creative responses and workshop pieces should be edited to this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of craft to study and critique
rubrics_metrics.description: The course centers on craft elements such as description, character, setting, dialogue, point of view, voice, stellar sentences, and revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Writer’s Toolkit handouts as models; critiques and creative responses should address these elements directly (e.g., how dialogue shapes character; how setting evokes sensory detail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment length expectations (varied)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific length expectations are given for each assignment type: e.g., 250 word introductions/reading responses in some weeks; ~250 word responses to selected readings; 350-400 word academic and creative responses; 5-6 pages for some workshop formats (nonfiction), 8-10 pages for the fiction workshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the week-by-week schedule for the required word/page counts; responses to peers are often ~350 words or one page depending on the course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop scheduling & live-session participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Weekly live Elluminate workshops will be held (typically Saturdays GMT/UTC 15:00-16:30) and run about one to two hours; sessions generally spend ~15 minutes discussing each workshop piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should attend these sessions and be prepared to discuss and receive feedback in real time. Attendance and engagement factor into participation grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision & final submission
rubrics_metrics.description: In the final week students are asked to review revision materials and revise one creative response or workshop essay and submit it to instructors by the stated deadline (e.g., Sunday, May 13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'Stellar Sentences' and 'Revision' handouts in the Writer’s Toolkit to guide edits; final revised pieces may be collected into a podcast anthology or e-book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read-as-writer approach
rubrics_metrics.description: All work will center on the idea of reading as a writer and generating creative work in response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responding to assigned readings, analyze authorial choices (form, structure, concision, tone, character) and apply those lessons to your own writing in creative responses and workshop pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing resources expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Final week instructors will post resources for publishing your work—the 'how to' of the industry—and some tools for revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should read and respond with questions about publishing; instructors provide guidance but engagement and questions are expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students with disabilities (accommodations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors will make reasonable accommodations for students with physical, mental or learning disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should contact the named instructor (or Student Disability Services) and obtain a Student Academic Accommodation Request form (SAAR) to specify reasonable course accommodations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic fraud / plagiarism policy
rubrics_metrics.description: You are expected to be honest and honorable in your fulfillment of assignments. Academic fraud is a serious form of misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An instructor who suspects academic fraud must inform the student in writing and may reduce the student's grade or assign an F; the instructor must write an account and a copy goes to the student who has the right to request a hearing. Full explanation provided in the Student Academic Handbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illness & excused absence policy
rubrics_metrics.description: University policy requires that students be permitted to make up examinations missed because of illness, mandatory religious obligations, certain University activities, or unavoidable circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors may request documentation before allowing make-up work. The syllabus reserves the right to request documentation if a student misses a substantial number of assignments due to illness.
